title: Qualified Services
description: Qualified services are conducting, directly supervising or directly supporting qualified research; at least 80% qualifying time makes all wages count.
summary: Qualified services are the employee activities whose wages count toward the U.S. federal R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41: conducting qualified research, first-line direct supervision of it, or direct support of it. Eligibility depends on what employees actually do, not job titles, and if at least 80% of an employee's service hours qualify, 100% of their wages qualify.

body.text: Qualified services are the employee activities whose wages count toward the U.S. federal R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41: conducting qualified research, first-line direct supervision of it, or direct support of it. Eligibility depends on what employees actually do, not job titles, and if at least 80% of an employee's service hours qualify, 100% of their wages qualify.

Qualified Services (QS) form the statutory core of employee wage claims under the U.S. federal Credit for Increasing Research Activities, codified in Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41). Within the statutory framework of Qualified Research Expenses (QREs)—which encompass In-House Research Expenses (IHREs) and Contract Research Expenses paid or incurred in carrying on a trade or business under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1)—wages paid or incurred to employees for Qualified Services under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) typically constitute the single largest expenditure component claimed by U.S. taxpayers. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c), eligible employee services are strictly confined to three functional categories: (1) engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(1)), (2) engaging in the immediate, first-line direct supervision of qualified research (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2)), and (3) engaging in the direct support of either persons conducting qualified research or persons directly supervising such research (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3)). Furthermore, under the "substantially all" rule of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2), if at least 80% of an employee's total service hours performed for the taxpayer during the taxable year consist of Qualified Services, 100% of that employee's taxable wages for the year qualify as IHREs.

Most notably, an employee's annual wages eligible to be claimed as IHREs are not capped by a "$250,000 limitation on FICA wages." Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(i), QRE "wages" are defined by cross-reference to 26 U.S.C. § 3401(a) (federal income tax withholding wages reported on Form W-2, Box 1), which imposes no per-employee dollar cap and is legally distinct from Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA) payroll tax wage base limits. The $250,000 statutory figure in IRC § 41 instead originally governed the aggregate annual election for a Qualified Small Business (QSB) to apply its research credit against employer payroll tax liabilities under 26 U.S.C. § 41(h)(4)(B)(i)(I)—an aggregate credit cap that Congress increased to $500,000 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022 under 26 U.S.C. § 41(h)(4)(B)(i)(II).

Furthermore, heightened Internal Revenue Service (IRS) procedural scrutiny on Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) and U.S. Tax Court precedent—including Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (decided December 23, 2024), Moore v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20, Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, and Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023)—establish strict operational boundaries for substantiating Qualified Services. Specifically, Section G of Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024; Instructions Rev. December 2025)—which requires taxpayers to disaggregate Qualified Services wages by discrete business component across Direct Research (Column 50), Direct Supervision (Column 51), and Direct Support (Column 52)—is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 and mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025 (subject to instruction guidelines). In parallel, for research credit refund claims on amended returns (operating under a transition perfection period extended through January 10, 2027), the IRS waived the initial filing requirement to list individual employee names and employee-specific discovery narratives on June 18, 2024 (FAQ 21), although granular employee-level and subcomponent-level documentation remains subject to demand during substantive IRS examination.
I. Statutory and Regulatory Foundation of Qualified Services
1.1 Qualified Research Expenses and the In-House Research Expense Component

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(a) and § 41(b)(1), a taxpayer's Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) equal the sum of In-House Research Expenses (§ 41(b)(1)(A)) and Contract Research Expenses (§ 41(b)(1)(B)) paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer. For startup ventures that have not yet commenced active commercial operations, 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(4) disregards the active trade or business requirement specifically for In-House Research Expenses if, at the time such expenses are paid or incurred, the taxpayer's principal purpose in making the expenditures is to use the results of the research in the active conduct of a future trade or business of the taxpayer (or of any other person who, together with the taxpayer, is treated as a single taxpayer under the controlled group aggregation rules of 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(1)). As the IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e. Research Tax Credit) IRC § 41 (IRS ATG, updated July 2, 2026) emphasizes, the statutory categories in IRC § 41(b) are exhaustive: if an expenditure is not explicitly set forth in Section 41(b), a taxpayer may not claim that expense as a QRE.
As codified in 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A), In-House Research Expenses comprise three exhaustive statutory categories:

items: Employee Wages for Qualified Services (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i)): Any wages paid or incurred to an employee for qualified services performed by such employee.

Supplies Used in Qualified Research (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and § 41(b)(2)(C)): Any amount paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C), the term "supplies" means any tangible property other than (i) land or improvements to land, and (ii) property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(b)(2)(i)–(ii) and the IRS ATG, general utility expenses (such as electricity used for general laboratory lighting) are treated as excluded general and administrative expenses, except to the extent the taxpayer establishes that the special character of the qualified research (such as high-energy laser or nuclear research) required extraordinary additional expenditures for utilities. Similarly, under IRS ATG Coordinated Issue Papers and Awareness Issues, examiners scrutinize "prototype" expenditures to verify that the property is not of a character subject to depreciation under 26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2, and exclude depreciation, overhead, employee benefits, and travel/entertainment relating to self-constructed assets.

Right to Use Computers in Qualified Research (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(b)(4)): Under regulations prescribed by the Secretary of the Treasury, any amount paid or incurred to another person for the right to use (time-sharing) computers in the conduct of qualified research. Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(b)(4), for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1985, amounts paid or incurred for the use of personal property are not QREs except for computer time-sharing payments where the computer is owned and operated by someone other than the taxpayer, located off the taxpayer's premises, and the taxpayer is not the primary user of the computer. Furthermore, under the flush language of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A), clause (iii) does not apply to any amount to the extent that the taxpayer (or any person aggregated with the taxpayer under § 41(f)(1)) receives or accrues any amount from any other person for the right to use substantially identical personal property.

body.text: 1.2 Statutory Definition of Wages and Correction of the FICA Wage Cap Misconception

Establishing an accurate and defensible Qualified Services claim begins with isolating the correct statutory wage base for each eligible employee prior to applying any time-allocation percentage. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(i), the term "wages" has the exact meaning given such term by 26 U.S.C. § 3401(a), which governs federal income tax withholding at the source. As confirmed by the IRS ATG (updated July 2, 2026) and 26 U.S.C. § 3401(a), this wage base includes all taxable remuneration for services performed by an employee for their employer that is subject to federal income tax withholding and reported in Box 1 of IRS Form W-2, including regular base salaries, bonuses, and taxable stock option redemptions/spreads upon exercise.

With respect to employee stock options, the IRS ATG—incorporating the judicial holdings in Apple Computer, Inc. v. Commissioner, 98 T.C. 232 (1992) and Sun Microsystems v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1995-69—establishes a two-step temporal rule when stock options are exercised and included in IRC § 3401(a) wages. Because an employee stock option is granted as compensation for services performed, whether the resulting option spread qualifies as an In-House Research Expense is determined by looking back to the grant year to evaluate whether the employee's services in that grant year constituted Qualified Services under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B); if the grant-year work qualified, the taxable spread amount is included in the research credit wage computation in the exercise year.

Conversely, remuneration that is excluded from federal income tax withholding under 26 U.S.C. § 3401(a)(1)–(23) is strictly excluded from QRE wages under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(i), even when paid to or on behalf of scientists and engineers engaged exclusively in qualified research. Specifically, non-taxable fringe benefits, health savings account (HSA) contributions, and pre-tax employee salary deferrals or employer matching contributions to a deferred compensation plan or trust under IRC § 401(a), § 401(k), or § 408(p) cannot be included in QRE wages. Indeed, the IRS maintains a dedicated Coordinated Issue Paper (Payments to a deferred compensation plan or trust such as a section 401(k) plan and matching employer's contributions) confirming that IRC § 401(k) contributions on behalf of research employees are not qualified research expenses under IRC § 41(b).

Two additional statutory provisions in 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D) modify the QRE wage base. First, for self-employed individuals and owner-employees within the meaning of 26 U.S.C. § 401(c)(1) (such as sole proprietors or partners performing services for an unincorporated trade or business), 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(ii) provides that the term "wages" includes the earned income (as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 401(c)(2)) of such employee. Second, to prevent a double federal tax benefit on the same labor dollars, 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(iii) mandates that QRE "wages" shall not include any amount taken into account in determining the Work Opportunity Tax Credit (WOTC) under 26 U.S.C. § 51(a). Under 26 U.S.C. § 51(a) and § 51(b)(1)–(3), the Work Opportunity Credit equals 40% of qualified first-year wages paid or incurred to individuals who are members of a targeted group, where qualified first-year wages taken into account per individual are capped at $6,000 per year generally, or $12,000, $14,000, or $24,000 per year for specific statutory categories of qualified veterans under § 51(b)(3). IRS Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024) enforces this statutory bar directly on Section F, Line 42 ("Total wages for qualified services for all business components (do not include any wages used in figuring the work opportunity credit)").

Statutory Correction of the "$250,000 FICA Wage Limitation" Claim: That statement is incorrect as a matter of federal tax law. Neither 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D) nor 26 U.S.C. § 3401(a) imposes a $250,000 cap—or any FICA wage base limitation—on an individual employee's qualified wages.

Instead, the $250,000 statutory figure in IRC § 41 originated in 26 U.S.C. § 41(h)(4)(B)(i)(I), which originally capped the aggregate annual research credit that a Qualified Small Business (QSB)—defined in 26 U.S.C. § 41(h)(3) as a corporation, partnership, or person with less than $5,000,000 in gross receipts for the taxable year and no gross receipts for any taxable year preceding the 5-taxable-year period ending with such taxable year—could elect to apply against its employer payroll tax liability. Furthermore, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(h)(4)(B)(i)(II), for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022, Congress increased this aggregate annual QSB payroll tax credit election limit by an additional $250,000, bringing the maximum annual payroll tax credit election to $500,000 (reflected on Form 6765, Section D, Line 34: "Enter the portion of line 28 elected as a payroll tax credit (do not enter more than $500,000)"). Consequently, taxpayers must reconcile Form W-2 Box 1 wages (IRC § 3401(a)) without any per-employee dollar ceiling, and apply the $500,000 ceiling under IRC § 41(h)(4)(B)(i)(II) solely at the aggregate credit election level when making a QSB payroll tax offset election in Section D of Form 6765.
1.3 Statutory and Regulatory Definition of Qualified Services
In the United States Code, 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) defines "qualified services" in two numbered clauses followed by the statutory "substantially all" flush language:

"The term 'qualified services' means services consisting of— (i) engaging in qualified research, or (ii) engaging in the direct supervision or direct support of research activities which constitute qualified research. If substantially all of the services performed by an individual for the taxpayer during the taxable year consists of services meeting the requirements of clause (i) or (ii), the term 'qualified services' means all of the services performed by such individual for the taxpayer during the taxable year."

In the official text of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B), direct supervision and direct support are combined within clause (ii). Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c) and the IRS ATG then subdivide IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) into three distinct regulatory categories: (1) Engaging in Qualified Research (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(1)), (2) Direct Supervision (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2)), and (3) Direct Support (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3)). Across all three regulatory categories, both the IRS ATG and U.S. Tax Court jurisprudence (Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201) enforce a strict functional standard: an employee's eligibility is determined solely by what the employee actually does during the taxable year, rather than by the employee's formal job title, written job description, or educational degree.
1.4 The Contingency Principle: Linking Qualified Services to the Four-Part Test (IRC § 41(d))

Because 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) defines Qualified Services by explicit reference to "qualified research," employee labor costs under IRC § 41(b) cannot qualify in isolation. As the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reaffirmed in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023) (affirming T.C. Memo. 2021-15), citing Shami v. Commissioner, 741 F.3d 560, 568 (5th Cir. 2014), quantifying QREs under IRC § 41(b) is a subordinate inquiry that is legally unreachable until the taxpayer establishes that qualified research occurred under IRC § 41(d): "Only after a taxpayer establishes that qualified research has occurred under Section 41(d) may we estimate, if needed, the amount of qualified research expenses under Section 41(b)."

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(1)–(2), an activity constitutes Qualified Research only if it satisfies all four statutory requirements—applied separately to each discrete business component under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(A) (where a "business component" is defined in § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer)—and is not excluded under § 41(d)(3)(B) or § 41(d)(4):

items: The Section 174 / Section 174A Expenditure and Uncertainty Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i) and § 1.174-2(a)(1)): The research activities must involve expenditures eligible for treatment as specified research or experimental expenditures. Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i) and § 1.174-2(a)(1), the expenditures must be incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense—meaning activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability or method for developing or improving a product or process, or the appropriate design of that product or process, based on information objectively available to the taxpayer at the start of the activities. For statutory currency, under Public Law 119-21 (the One Big Beautiful Bill Act), for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) was updated to reference domestic research or experimental expenditures under newly enacted 26 U.S.C. § 174A, which permits immediate deduction under § 174A(a) or an election to capitalize and amortize ratably over at least 60 months under § 174A(c).

The Discovering Technological Information Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(3)–(4)): The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature. Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(4), information is technological in nature if the process of experimentation used to discover such information fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Pursuant to final regulations issued in Treasury Decision (T.D.) 9104 (effective January 2, 2004, applicable to taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003, codified at 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) and (a)(4)), a taxpayer is not required to seek information that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the particular field of science or engineering, is not required to succeed in developing the new or improved business component, and may employ existing technologies and rely on existing scientific, engineering, or computer science principles. Under the patent safe harbor of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii), the issuance of a patent by the Patent and Trademark Office under 35 U.S.C. § 151 (other than a design patent under 35 U.S.C. § 171) is conclusive evidence that a taxpayer has discovered information that is technological in nature intended to eliminate uncertainty, though a patent is not a precondition for credit availability. Conversely, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(7) states that the mere employment of computers or information technology to store, collect, manipulate, translate, disseminate, produce, distribute, or process data or information does not by itself establish that qualified research has been undertaken.

The Business Component and Permitted Purpose Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(3); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii)): The application of the discovered technological information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(ii)), and the research must be undertaken for a qualified purpose—meaning it relates to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component (§ 41(d)(3)(A); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii)). Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(B) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), research will not be treated as conducted for a qualified purpose if it relates to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors.

The Process of Experimentation (POE) Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6)): Substantially all of the research activities with respect to the business component must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), a process of experimentation is a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities. Even if there is no uncertainty concerning capability or method, a taxpayer may undertake a process of experimentation if the appropriate design of the desired result is uncertain as of the beginning of the research activities. To satisfy 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), the process must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science and involves three core elements: (a) the identification of uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of the business component, (b) the identification of one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty, and (c) the identification and conduct of a process of evaluating the alternatives (through, for example, modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial-and-error methodology).

body.text: Distinguishing the Two Statutory "Substantially All" (80%) Rules: Tax practitioners and auditors must carefully distinguish between the "substantially all" rule of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) (for the Process of Experimentation test) and the "substantially all" rule of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) (for employee Qualified Services wages). As codified in 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) and noted in Footnote 8 of the IRS ATG, the "substantially all" requirement of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) is satisfied only if 80% or more of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to a business component, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (and without regard to the employee wage 80% rule of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2)), constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose under IRC § 41(d)(3). If 80% or more of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to a business component constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose, the POE test is satisfied even if the remaining 20% or less of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to the business component do not constitute elements of a process of experimentation, so long as those remaining research activities satisfy IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and are not otherwise excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4).

The Shrinking-Back Rule (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2)): When an overall discrete business component fails to satisfy the four-part test of IRC § 41(d)(1), 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2) directs that the requirements be applied at the "most significant subset of elements" of the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used in the taxpayer's trade or business. This shrinking back continues until either a subset of elements of the product that satisfies the requirements is reached, or the most basic element of the product is reached and fails to satisfy the test. As clarified in T.D. 9104, the shrinking-back rule is applied only if the overall business component fails IRC § 41(d)(1), and is not itself applied as a reason to exclude research activities from credit eligibility. However, for employee wages to be claimed under a shrinking-back analysis, the taxpayer's records must separate qualified and non-qualified employee activities and wage costs at the specific subcomponent level.
II. Detailed Regulatory Analysis of the Three Qualified Services Categories

Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c) establishes strict functional boundaries for each of the three categories of Qualified Services, separating eligible technical and experimental work from excluded routine, higher-tier managerial, and general and administrative (G&A) activities.
2.1 Engaging in Qualified Research (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(1))

Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(1), the term "engaging in qualified research" as used in 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) means the actual conduct of qualified research, illustrated in the regulation by "a scientist conducting laboratory experiments."

Even when performed by technical personnel within an R&D department, time spent on activities excluded from Qualified Research under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4), 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c), and 26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2(a)(3) does not constitute Qualified Services and must be tracked and removed. Specifically, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c)(2) exclude research conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component (once it meets basic functional and economic requirements), which the IRS ATG notes includes preproduction planning for a finished component, tooling up for production, trial production runs, troubleshooting production equipment faults, accumulating production process data, and debugging flaws. However, under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii) (and Tax Court precedent such as Union Carbide), the commercial production exclusion applies separately to the activities relating to the development of a product and the activities relating to the development of the manufacturing process; thus, even after a product meets the taxpayer's basic functional and economic requirements, activities relating to the development of the manufacturing process may still constitute qualified research if the process development independently satisfies IRC § 41(d) prior to being ready for commercial use. Similarly, under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iv), clinical testing of a pharmaceutical product prior to its commercial production in the United States (even if commercially available in other countries), or additional clinical testing after Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval undertaken to establish new FDA-approved functional uses, characteristics, indications, combinations, dosages, or delivery forms, is not treated as occurring after the beginning of commercial production.

Furthermore, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(B) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c)(3) exclude activities relating to adapting an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need (though this exclusion does not apply merely because a business component is intended for a specific customer), and as illustrated in T.D. 9104, wages paid to employees to adapt an existing core software program to a customer's requirements do not constitute In-House Research Expenses under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A). Likewise, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(C) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c)(4) exclude duplicating or reproducing an existing business component in whole or in part from a physical examination of the component itself or from plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information (such as reverse engineering), though examining an existing component in the course of developing the taxpayer's own component does not trigger the exclusion.

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(D), 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c)(5), and 26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2(a)(3), excluded non-qualified activities also include efficiency surveys, activities relating to management functions or techniques (such as preparation of financial data and analysis, development of employee training programs and management organization plans, and management-based changes in production processes such as rearranging workstations on an assembly line), market research, testing, or development (including advertising or promotions), routine data collections, and routine or ordinary testing or inspections for quality control or assurance. In addition, an IRS Coordinated Issue Paper cited in Section 10 of the IRS ATG (Technical writers and other individuals who prepared end user manuals or other instructive documents for the end user) confirms that wages paid to technical writers, editors, illustrators, or engineers for preparing end-user manuals, instructive documents for end users, or general customer support are excluded from QREs. Finally, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(E)–(H) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c)(6)–(9) exclude internal-use software (unless meeting a regulatory exception under § 1.41-4(c)(6)(ii) or satisfying the high threshold of innovation test under § 1.41-4(c)(6)(i)(C), with routine installation, customization, enhancement, and maintenance of vendor-supplied software excluded per the IRS ATG Coordinated Issue Paper on Internal-Use Software), foreign research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States, research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities, and research funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity where the taxpayer does not bear financial risk or retain substantial rights in the research results (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)).
2.2 Direct Supervision (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2))
Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2), the term "direct supervision" as used in 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) is defined as follows:

"The term 'direct supervision' as used in section 41(b)(2)(B) means the immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research (as in the case of a research scientist who directly supervises laboratory experiments, but who may not actually perform experiments). 'Direct supervision' does not include supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report, even if that manager is a qualified research scientist."

This regulatory text establishes two strict compliance boundaries, and "Management above the first-line manager level" is specifically flagged as a non-qualifying Awareness Issue in Section 10 of the IRS ATG. First, supervisory oversight qualifies as "direct supervision" only at the immediate, first-line management tier directly overseeing the personnel conducting the qualified research. As reported in The Tax Adviser, in Moore v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20, the U.S. Tax Court disallowed a portion of the wages claimed for an S corporation's president and chief operating officer ("Mr. Robert," an engineer by trade) in part because he was not the first-line manager of the company's engineers, excluding his managerial role from "direct supervision" under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2). However, as the IRS ATG and practitioner analyses in The Tax Adviser and Moss Adams (citing Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201) explain, while higher-level research managers cannot claim time spent supervising first-line managers, if a higher-level manager or executive with technical expertise personally performs hands-on research tasks—such as brainstorming technical solutions, participating in technical and design review meetings, designing experiments, or directly supervising researchers without an intermediate manager—that specific fraction of the executive's time qualifies as either engaging in qualified research (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(1)) or direct supervision (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2)) based on the actual tasks performed.

Second, even for a first-line R&D supervisor, only the portion of time dedicated to technical direction and immediate oversight of the experimentation—such as reviewing code or experimental designs, directing testing protocols, and evaluating technical alternatives—is eligible as Direct Supervision. Time spent by a supervisory employee on general Human Resources (HR) tasks (such as annual performance evaluations, general staff scheduling, or non-experimental training) or financial/administrative duties (such as non-experimental budget approvals) is excluded General and Administrative time.
2.3 Direct Support (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3))

Direct Support is one of the most frequently contested areas during IRS examinations because the taxpayer must demonstrate an immediate operational nexus between the support service and the conduct of qualified research. Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3), the term "direct support" as used in 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) means services in the direct support of either (i) persons engaging in actual conduct of qualified research, or (ii) persons who are directly supervising persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research. At the same time, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3) specifies that "Direct support does not include supervision. Supervisory services constitute 'qualified services' only to the extent provided in paragraph (c)(2) of this section."

Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3) and the IRS ATG establish a bright line between qualifying hands-on support and non-qualifying indirect or administrative services through four explicit qualifying examples and five excluded examples. Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3), qualifying Direct Support includes: (1) the services of a machinist for machining a part of an experimental model used in qualified research, (2) the services of a secretary for typing reports describing laboratory results derived from qualified research, (3) the services of a laboratory worker for cleaning equipment used in qualified research, and (4) the services of a clerk for compiling research data (such as organizing raw data from formulation or prototype trials). Additionally, in Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201, the Tax Court accepted small, substantiated time allocations for non-R&D personnel (such as quality assurance and shipping/handling staff) who directly assisted product development engineers.

Conversely, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3) mandates that Direct Support does not include general administrative services or other services only indirectly of benefit to research activities, "whether general administrative personnel are part of the research department or in a separate department." Specifically excluded under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3) and Section 10 of the IRS ATG are: (1) payroll personnel preparing salary checks of laboratory scientists, (2) an accountant accounting for research expenses, (3) a janitor performing general cleaning of a research laboratory (as opposed to a laboratory worker cleaning specialized laboratory equipment used in qualified research), (4) officers or administrative staff supervising financial or personnel matters, general secretarial work, arranging travel, or managing general office supplies, and (5) in-house attorneys performing legal services and patent procurement activities.

body.text: III. Wage Allocation Mechanics and the "Substantially All" (80%) Rule
3.1 Proportional Allocation (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1)) vs. Full Inclusion (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2))

Once an employee's activities are mapped to the three categories of Qualified Services, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d) governs how the employee's IRC § 3401(a) wages are allocated to In-House Research Expenses. Under the general proportional allocation rule of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1), if an employee has performed both Qualified Services and non-qualified services during the taxable year, only the amount of wages allocated to the performance of Qualified Services constitutes an IHRE. In the absence of another method of allocation that the taxpayer can demonstrate to be more appropriate, the regulation directs that the IHRE wage amount is determined by multiplying the total amount of IRC § 3401(a) wages paid to or incurred for the employee during the taxable year by the ratio of the total time actually spent by the employee in the performance of Qualified Services for the taxpayer to the total time spent by the employee in the performance of all services for the taxpayer during the taxable year (Allocation Ratio = Hours Spent in Qualified Services ÷ Total Hours Spent in All Services).

As the IRS ATG clarifies, this fraction is evaluated on an employee-by-employee basis using hours actually spent performing services—meaning paid non-working time, such as sick leave, holidays, and vacation, is excluded from the fraction. If an engineer has 2,080 total paid hours in the year, 160 of which are for vacation and holidays, the Total Service Hours in the denominator are 1,920 hours (2,080 minus 160); if the engineer logs 1,550 hours performing Qualified Services, the resulting Qualified Services ratio is 80.73% (1,550 ÷ 1,920, meeting the 80% threshold), whereas 1,450 hours yields 75.52% (1,450 ÷ 1,920, failing the 80% threshold).

Notwithstanding the general proportional rule, the flush language of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2) establish the "substantially all" rule: if at least 80% of an employee's wages (allocated on the time-ratio basis of § 1.41-2(d)(1)) during the taxable year are for Qualified Services meeting the requirements of IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(i) or (ii), then the term "qualified services" means all (100%) of the services performed by that employee for the taxpayer during the taxable year. If the employee's ratio of Qualified Services hours to total service hours is less than 80%, the "substantially all" rule does not apply, and only the actual proportional percentage of wages may be claimed under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1).
3.2 Mathematical Precision and Audit Vulnerability of the 80% Threshold
Recomputing the arithmetic step by step clarifies both the exact relative gain at the 80% threshold and the severe cliff risk under IRS audit.

Hypothetical Worked Example 1 (The 80% Threshold vs. 79% Audit Cliff): Assume a hypothetical software engineer earns $100,000 in taxable W-2 Box 1 wages (IRC § 3401(a)) and works 2,000 actual service hours (excluding sick leave and vacation) during the taxable year. At exactly 80% Qualified Services time (1,600 qualified hours and 400 non-qualified G&A hours), a purely proportional allocation under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1) would yield $80,000 in QRE wages ($100,000 × 0.80). Because the employee meets the 80% threshold of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2), 100% of annual wages ($100,000 × 1.00 = $100,000) qualify as IHREs. This adds $20,000 in claimable QRE wages, which represents a 20-percentage-point gain in total annual wages captured, or a 25.0% relative increase in QREs ($20,000 ÷ $80,000 = +25.0%) compared to an $80,000 proportional allocation. Conversely, defending a 100% wage claim under the 80% rule hinges on substantiating that non-qualified time (G&A, routine testing, or post-production maintenance) did not exceed 20%. If an IRS examiner reclassifies just 20 hours (1% of annual working hours) from direct support to non-qualified G&A—increasing non-qualified time from 20% (400 hours) to 21% (420 hours) and reducing Qualified Services time from 80% to 79% (1,580 hours)—the claim loses the "substantially all" bonus and drops to proportional allocation ($100,000 × 0.79 = $79,000), resulting in an immediate $21,000 disallowance (21% of annual wages lost due to a 1-percentage-point adjustment).

Hypothetical Worked Example 2 (Engineering Manager Direct Supervision Leverage): Suppose a first-line Engineering Manager earns $150,000 in annual IRC § 3401(a) wages while overseeing 5 software developers (each earning $100,000). During the taxable year, the manager spends 25% of actual working hours writing experimental code (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(1)), 60% of actual working hours reviewing code and directing technical architecture as immediate first-line supervision (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2)), and 15% of actual working hours on general HR administration (non-qualified G&A). If the taxpayer mistakenly counts only the manager's hands-on coding time (25%), the manager falls short of the 80% rule and generates only $37,500 in claimable QRE wages ($150,000 × 0.25), leaving $112,500 excluded. By properly documenting both hands-on coding (25%) and first-line Direct Supervision (60%), the manager's combined Qualified Services ratio reaches 85% (25% + 60%). Because 85% ≥ 80%, the "substantially all" rule (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2)) triggers 100% wage inclusion, yielding $150,000 in claimable QRE wages ($0 excluded)—an increase of $112,500 (+300%) in qualified wage QREs for that single employee.

body.text: IV. Procedural Scrutiny, Form 6765 Section G, and Tax Court Jurisprudence
4.1 Upfront Disclosure on IRS Form 6765 and Refund Claim Prerequisites

On Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024), Section D (Lines 33a–36) governs the Qualified Small Business payroll tax credit election under IRC § 41(h), instructing the filer on Line 34 not to enter more than $500,000 and carrying the elected amount to Form 8974. Section E (Other Information, Lines 37–41)—which must be completed whenever QREs are reported on Line 48—requires taxpayers to disclose the total number of business components generating QREs (Line 37), the exact dollar amount of officers' wages included on Line 42 (Line 38, providing examiners an immediate audit flag for executive wage claims under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2)), whether the taxpayer acquired or disposed of any major portion of a trade or business in the tax year (Line 39), whether any new categories of expenses were included as current-year QREs (Line 40), and whether any QREs were determined following the ASC 730 Directive (Line 41). In Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary, Lines 42–48), Line 42 captures total wages for Qualified Services across all business components (explicitly instructing filers not to include any wages used in figuring the Work Opportunity Credit under IRC § 51), Line 43 captures total supply costs, Line 44 captures computer rental or lease costs, Line 45 captures the applicable amount of contract research expenses, Line 46 captures basic research payments, Line 47 sums Lines 45 and 46, and Line 48 sums Lines 42, 43, 44, and 47.

Most significantly for Qualified Services substantiation, Section G (Business Component Information, Columns 49–56) requires taxpayers to report component-by-component QRE data for the business components comprising at least 80% of total QREs, up to a maximum of 50 business components ("80%/Top 50"), with any remaining business components reported in aggregate on a single row by entering "Aggregate Business Components" in Column 49(c) (leaving Columns 49(a), 49(b), 49(d), 49(e), and 49(f) blank for that line). If statistical sampling was used under Rev. Proc. 2011-42, the filer must append the word "sample" to the business component identifier in Column 49(c) for sampled units and attach Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf. Across Columns 49(a)–(f), the taxpayer identifies the EIN of the controlled group member conducting the research (Column 49(a)), the entity's Principal Business Activity (PBA) code (Column 49(b)), the business component's name or unique alphanumeric identifier matching the taxpayer's books and records (Column 49(c)), the business component type selected from 1. Product, 2. Process, or 3. All Others (Column 49(d)), the software type if applicable selected from A. IUS, B. DFS, C. Non-IUS, or D. Excepted from IUS treatment (Column 49(e)), and—only when claiming a new or increased research credit on an amended return—a narrative describing the information sought to be discovered (Column 49(f), which is not required on timely filed original returns including extensions). Section G then requires taxpayers to disaggregate their in-house Qualified Services wages for each reported business component across four specific columns:

body.text: Per the Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025), Section G is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026, and becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025 (subject to instruction guidelines).

In parallel, for research credit claims filed on amended returns or claims for refund, the IRS instituted five mandatory upfront disclosure items effective for claims postmarked on or after January 10, 2022 (following Field Attorney Advice FAA 20214101F and IR-2021-203, issued in October 2021). On June 18, 2024 (via FAQ 21 on IRS.gov, Research Credit Claims (Section 41) on Amended Returns Frequently Asked Questions, updated through October 1, 2026), the IRS waived two of those five requirements at the time of initial refund claim filing—specifically waiving the requirement to list (a) the names of the individuals who performed each research activity and (b) the information each individual sought to discover, though both remain subject to request if the claim is selected for examination (and under FAQ 10 and FAQ 11, taxpayers identifying individuals may list job titles or positions with exact headcounts and group employees seeking to discover the same information for a business component). Consequently, a valid research credit refund claim must provide at filing: (1) all business components to which the Section 41 claim relates for that year, (2) all research activities performed for each business component, and (3) total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year (which may be provided using Form 6765). During the multi-year transition period (extended through January 10, 2027), taxpayers submitting a deficient refund claim receive Letter 6426C or Letter 6428 and have 45 days to perfect the claim by fax or paper mail (portable electronic storage devices are not accepted per FAQ 9); claims rejected as deficient or unprocessable are not eligible for challenge before the IRS Independent Office of Appeals (FAQ 7, FAQ 8, FAQ 9, FAQ 12, and FAQ 15).
4.2 Lessons from Tax Court Jurisprudence: Phoenix Design Group and Wage Substantiation Case Law

Judicial precedent confirms that tracking employee hours is legally insufficient if the underlying project fails the four-part test of IRC § 41(d) or if the taxpayer's records fail to link employee tasks to specific business components and technical uncertainties.
1. Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (Docket No. 4759-22, Decided December 23, 2024)

In Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, the U.S. Tax Court examined research tax credits claimed by Phoenix Design Group, Inc. (PDG), a Tennessee C corporation specializing in designing mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection (MEPF) systems for hospitals, laboratories, and educational buildings. As reported in legal analyses of the opinion by Cherry Bekaert, PDG engaged a consultant in 2017 to perform a research credit study using project documentation from 2012–2016, claiming research credits generated in tax years 2013 through 2016 ($138,205 in 2013; $158,031 in 2014; $138,334 in 2015; and $128,228 in 2016) that were utilized in tax years 2015 through 2019 (resulting in notice deficiencies of $55,504 in 2015; $47,811 in 2016; $219,177 in 2017; $68,147 in 2018; and $71,102 in 2019), with the claimed credits attributable solely to employee wages. Case analyses by Grant Thornton and Cherry Bekaert clarify the exact procedural posture: following an August 29, 2023 Tax Court order, the parties agreed to try a non-binding judgment sample of three representative trial projects—(1) Gerald Champion Military Psychiatric Unit, (2) Baptist Memorial Health North Mississippi Oxford (BMHNMO), and (3) Vanderbilt University Engineering and Science Building (VUESB)—selected from 238 claimed projects (out of 409 to 419 total projects), and excluded the quantification of QRE dollar amounts from the trial's scope. However, the parties stipulated that if none of the three trial projects involved qualified research, PDG would be liable for 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662 across the deficiency years ($11,101 for 2015; $9,021 for 2016; $43,835 for 2017; $13,629 for 2018; and $14,220 for 2019).

Although the Commissioner conceded the Technological Information test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i)) and the general Business Component requirement (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(3)), the Tax Court held that PDG failed to establish both the Section 174 Uncertainty test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)) and the Process of Experimentation test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C)) for all three trial projects, sustaining the 20% accuracy-related penalties. First, the court rejected PDG's argument that technical design uncertainty persisted beyond the delivery of stamped construction documents until construction was complete simply because designs could be revised during construction, holding that performing standard engineering calculations, complying with building codes, or adapting designs to client equipment selections does not show that available information failed to establish an appropriate design at the outset. Second, the court rejected the contention that following a standardized six-stage American Institute of Architects (AIA) / MEPF design workflow (Basis of Design, Schematic Design, Design Development, Construction Documents, Bidding, and Construction Administration) inherently constituted a systematic Process of Experimentation. Comparing witness testimony against employee hour sheets, the court found that generic time-sheet narratives did not categorize hours by design phase, did not align with work completed in each stage, and did not show a systematic evaluation of alternatives to resolve technical uncertainty. Third, as reported in analyses by Cherry Bekaert, the court explained that under the shrinking-back rule (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2)), uncertainty in a single sub-element (such as final equipment for a hybrid operating room) does not automatically create design uncertainty for an entire building's MEPF system, and if an overall building project fails the four-part test, it can shrink back to a smaller subsystem or engineering discipline (mechanical, electrical, or plumbing), but cannot shrink back to a specific design phase or to the activities of specific individual employees. Because PDG failed to provide component-level documentation delineating qualified versus non-qualified employee activities and wage costs for discrete subcomponents, the shrinking-back rule could not rescue the wage claims.
2. Corroborating Federal Jurisprudence on Qualified Services Substantiation
Additional federal court decisions analyzed in The Tax Adviser and the Seventh Circuit's opinion in Little Sandy Coal reinforce the evidentiary rules governing Qualified Services wage allocations:

Engineering firm wage QREs across 3 sampled MEPF projects (out of 238 claimed); linkage to IRC § 41(d) POE and shrink-back rule (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2)).

Disallowed & 20% IRC § 6662 penalties sustained: Generic hour sheets and linear 6-stage AIA design phases failed to prove technical uncertainty or a POE; shrink-back applies to system subcomponents, not individual employees or design phases, and requires subcomponent wage segregation.
Moore v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20
S corporation president/COO ("Mr. Robert") wage QREs under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(1)–(3) across 4 sample projects.

Partially disallowed: Record failed to separate qualified research from broader new product development (e.g., specifying product requirements); COO was not the first-line manager of engineers, disqualifying his oversight from "direct supervision."
Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84
Estimation of employee wage QREs under the Cohan rule without component-level evidence where contemporaneous proposals showed uncertainties were resolved.

Disallowed: Courts will not apply the Cohan rule to estimate wages where the taxpayer fails to make a threshold showing that an employee performed qualified services on a specific business component; trial testimony cannot overcome contrary contemporaneous records.
Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023)
Interaction between IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) 80% POE rule and IRC § 41(b) wage estimation for Corn Island Shipyard shipbuilding activities.

Disallowed: Oral testimony without contemporaneous records failed to prove 80% of research activities constituted a POE (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6)); QRE wages under § 41(b) cannot be estimated until § 41(d) qualification is established.
Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201
Executive time estimates prepared by Senior VP of Product Operations (Harvey Wende) and job-title vs. actual-activity standard.

Allowed: Actual yearly activities, not job titles, determine QS eligibility; high-level executives who personally perform or directly supervise research and non-R&D staff providing direct support (QA, shipping/handling) can qualify when supported by credible institutional testimony and corroborating evidence.
Shami v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2012-78, aff'd, 741 F.3d 560 (5th Cir. 2014)
Uncorroborated executive wage QRE estimates for CEO and vice president.

Disallowed: Time estimates rejected where witness testimonies were contradictory and noncredible, executives lacked technical backgrounds in science or engineering, and no corroborating documentary evidence existed.
Fudim v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1994-235
Time allocations (≥80% claims) without formal time-tracking logs for rapid UV-light polymer modeling research.

Allowed in part, disallowed in part: Cohan rule applied to allow ≥80% time allocations for Mr. and Mrs. Fudim supported by strong corroborating evidence (patents, published scientific articles, technical backgrounds, and credible testimony), while disallowing unsupported time claimed for their daughter.

body.text: 4.3 Substantiation Standards: Contemporaneous Records vs. Estimation (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d) and IRC § 6001)

Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d) (T.D. 9104) and 26 U.S.C. § 6001 (governed by 26 C.F.R. § 1.6001-1), a taxpayer claiming a credit under IRC § 41 must retain permanent books of account and records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit. Failure to maintain records in accordance with these rules is an independent legal basis for disallowing the credit, and IRS examiners are authorized under 26 C.F.R. § 1.6001-1(d) to issue a formal Notice of Inadequate Records via Letter 978 (DO) (Notice of Inadequate Records), Letter 979 (DO) (Inadequate Record Notice), or Letter 1022 (DO) (Inadequate Records Notice Follow-up).

Primary IRS guidance in the IRS ATG (Substantiation and Recordkeeping, updated July 2, 2026) and judicial precedent define the exact legal boundary. First, the IRS ATG explicitly instructs examiners that the IRS is not required to accept estimates of qualified research expenses if documentation exists to verify the actual amount of such expenses. Second, courts permit a taxpayer to use an estimation method (under Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930)) only when contemporaneous records do not exist, and only if two strict conditions are met: (1) the taxpayer first establishes with corroborating evidence that it actually engaged in qualified research activities on a specific business component as defined in IRC § 41(d), and (2) the failure to maintain a proper system to capture the relevant information is not an "inexactitude... of their own making," restricting estimation methods solely to cases where the only remaining issue is the exact dollar amount paid or incurred during the qualified research activity, with factual support for every assumption underlying the estimates.

To reduce recordkeeping disputes proactively, Notice 2004-11 (published February 9, 2004, 2004-6 I.R.B.) permits Large Business and International (LB&I, formerly LMSB) taxpayers and the IRS to enter into a prospective Research Credit Recordkeeping Agreement (RCRA)—typically proposed at the conclusion of an examination cycle with the examiner and Computer Audit Specialist (CAS)—to establish upfront what specific records will substantiate future research credit claims (though an RCRA does not resolve substantive activity eligibility under IRC § 41(d)). Additionally, when employee or business-component populations are large, taxpayers may utilize statistical sampling strictly in accordance with Rev. Proc. 2011-42 (2011-37 I.R.B. 318), attaching the sampling plan (Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf) when required under Form 6765 Section G.
V. Best Practices and Strategic Next Steps for Substantiating Qualified Services
5.1 Granular Time Tracking Systems (TTS) and Activity-to-Component Mapping

To satisfy 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d), 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d), and the business-component reporting structure of Form 6765 Section G (Columns 49–53), a taxpayer's Time Tracking System (TTS) must capture more than aggregate payroll hours or broad departmental cost centers. Time entries should simultaneously link each employee's hours across three dimensions: (a) the discrete business component or subcomponent (IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2)), matching the unique alphanumeric identifier in Form 6765 Column 49(c); (b) the specific Qualified Services category—Direct Conduct of Research (Form 6765, Column 50), Direct Supervision (Column 51), Direct Support (Column 52), or Excluded Non-Qualified/G&A activity; and (c) the specific experimental phase or hypothesis being evaluated (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)).

Integrating time-tracking software with engineering and software project management platforms (such as Agile sprint tickets, engineering change requests, CAD revision logs, and laboratory notebooks) provides contemporaneous corroboration that the hours logged were genuinely tied to resolving technical uncertainty rather than routine maintenance or code compliance. For employees hovering near the 70%–85% Qualified Services range, tracking both qualified Direct Support tasks and non-qualified G&A/post-production tasks is essential to determine whether the employee legitimately crosses the 80% threshold of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2) (after excluding sick leave, holidays, and vacation from the denominator per the IRS ATG) and to defend against a 1-percentage-point audit reclassification cliff.
5.2 Annual Functional Role Mapping and Internal Audit Checklist

Because the IRS ATG and Tax Court precedent (Suder, T.C. Memo. 2014-201; Moore, T.C. Memo. 2023-20) reject reliance on job titles, taxpayers should conduct an annual functional analysis across technical, supervisory, and support personnel through cross-functional collaboration among engineering leadership, human resources, payroll, and tax compliance teams. An audit-ready annual substantiation file for In-House Research Expenses should contain the following four core documentation packages:

items: Form W-2 Box 1 Payroll Segregation and Reconciliation Workpapers: Detailed employee-by-employee schedules reconciling Form W-2 Box 1 taxable wages under 26 U.S.C. § 3401(a) (or IRC § 401(c)(2) earned income for self-employed individuals under § 41(b)(2)(D)(ii)), evaluating grant-year qualification for exercised stock options (Apple Computer / Sun Microsystems), isolating officer wages for Form 6765 Section E (Line 38), and removing any wages used to compute the Work Opportunity Credit under 26 U.S.C. § 51(a) (IRC § 41(b)(2)(D)(iii) and Form 6765 Section F, Line 42). Rather than applying a $250,000 FICA cap to individual employee wages, taxpayers should apply the $500,000 QSB cap under IRC § 41(h)(4)(B)(i)(II) only at the aggregate credit election level if the taxpayer is an eligible Qualified Small Business electing the payroll tax offset in Section D (Line 34) of Form 6765.

Contemporaneous Technical Project Narratives and Subcomponent Evidence: Business-component documentation establishing all four tests of IRC § 41(d)(1)—specifically identifying the technical uncertainty at the outset (IRC § 174 / § 174A), the alternatives evaluated, and the iterative testing or modeling conducted (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)), structured so that if an overall system fails, costs and hours can be shrunk back to discrete mechanical, electrical, or software subcomponents under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2).

Contemporaneous Time Allocation Logs and Corroborating Business Records: Daily or weekly electronic time sheets, project logs, calendars, appointment books, design review minutes, and performance evaluations supporting the exact ratio of Qualified Services hours to total service hours worked (excluding vacation, holidays, and sick leave) under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1)–(2).

Functional Interviews and Contemporary Declarations: Documented functional interviews and signed confirmations from technical personnel and first-line supervisors verifying their task allocations and distinguishing qualified Direct Supervision and Direct Support from excluded higher-level management and G&A duties.

body.text: 5.3 Strategic Governance and Regulatory Clarification Initiatives

items: Enterprise-Wide R&D Governance Committee: Establish an enterprise-wide R&D Governance Committee uniting engineering/scientific leaders, finance/tax, and human resources to standardize internal definitions around 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c), preventing technical personnel from misclassifying general departmental overhead or higher-tier management as Qualified Services out of organizational convenience.

Automated Project-Management and Payroll Tracking Integration: Prioritize automated tracking integration linking payroll, time-tracking software, and task-level project management tools (for example, logging hours to specific experimental tasks such as designing an experiment, testing a prototype failure mode, or analyzing trial data), directly addressing the evidentiary deficiencies highlighted in Phoenix Design Group (T.C. Memo. 2024-113) and the component-level disaggregation required by Form 6765 Section G.

Industry Advocacy for Formal IRS Guidance on Digital Direct Support Roles: The explicit examples of Direct Support in 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3)—typing lab reports, cleaning lab equipment, compiling research data, and machining parts of an experimental model—reflect physical laboratory and manufacturing paradigms. In modern software and digital R&D, specialized personnel such as dedicated cloud environment engineers who build and maintain isolated computational testbeds or DevOps engineers who manage continuous integration/continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines used exclusively for experimental software builds operate on the boundary between qualified Direct Support (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3)) and excluded general IT maintenance. Engaging with the Treasury Department and the IRS through industry associations to request formal administrative guidance (such as Revenue Procedures or Notices) clarifying 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3) for digital research support roles would reduce audit uncertainty.

Recurrent Process-of-Experimentation and Qualified Services Compliance Training: Implement mandatory, recurrent POE and Qualified Services compliance training for engineers, scientists, and project managers so that technical staff understand the legal boundary between routine engineering/code compliance and a systematic Process of Experimentation (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)), fortifying the contemporaneous records generated during research execution.

cells: IRC § 41 codifies the federal Credit for Increasing Research Activities; IRC § 41(b)(1) defines QREs as the sum of In-House Research Expenses (IHREs) and Contract Research Expenses incurred in carrying on a trade or business.
26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1)(A)–(B), with the § 41(b)(4) startup trade or business exception for IHREs.

Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A), IHREs consist of: (i) wages paid or incurred to an employee for qualified services, (ii) supplies used in the conduct of qualified research, and (iii) under regulations, amounts paid to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research.

IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) defines "qualified services" as: (i) engaging in qualified research, or (ii) engaging in the direct supervision or direct support of research activities which constitute qualified research.
The statute contains two clauses ((i) and (ii)), while 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(1)–(3) divides them into three regulatory prongs.

Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and IRS regulations, if "substantially all" (defined as at least 80%) of an employee's services for the taxpayer during the taxable year consist of qualified services, 100% of the employee's wages for the year qualify.

Core 80% rule in 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2). Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1) and the IRS ATG, the denominator is total hours spent in the performance of all services, excluding sick leave, holidays, and vacation.

Under the 80% rule, "100% of that employee's annual wages (up to the $250,000 limitation on FICA wages) are eligible to be claimed as IHREs," and taxpayers must calculate "the FICA wage base for each claimed employee."
26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(i), § 3401(a), and § 41(h)(4)(B)(i)(I)–(II) (Law in force; § 41(h) limit increased for tax years beginning after Dec. 31, 2022)

Major Factual Correction: IRC § 41(b)(2)(D)(i) defines QRE wages via IRC § 3401(a) (Form W-2 Box 1 income tax withholding wages), which has no $250,000 per-employee cap and is not FICA wages. The $250,000 figure was the pre-2023 aggregate cap on the Qualified Small Business (QSB) payroll tax credit election under IRC § 41(h)(4)(B)(i)(I), which increased to $500,000 for tax years beginning after Dec. 31, 2022 (§ 41(h)(4)(B)(i)(II)).

Meeting the 80% threshold leads to a "20% increase in QREs compared to a proportional allocation at exactly the 80% mark," while 21% non-qualified time defaults the claim to 79% proportional allocation.

Moving from 80% proportional allocation ($80,000) to 100% inclusion ($100,000) adds 20 percentage points of total annual wages, which equals a 25.0% relative increase in QREs ((100% − 80%) ÷ 80% = +25.0%). Dropping from 80% to 79% reduces QRE wages by 21 percentage points ($21,000 on $100,000).
Four-Part Test under IRC § 41(d): (1) Section 174 test, (2) Technological information test, (3) Business component test, and (4) Process of experimentation (POE) test.
26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A)–(C); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(2)–(6); P.L. 119-21 (IRC § 174A effective for tax years beginning after Dec. 31, 2024)
Under P.L. 119-21 (One Big Beautiful Bill Act), for tax years beginning after Dec. 31, 2024, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) cross-references domestic R&E expenditures under new IRC § 174A.

Engaging in Qualified Research (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(1)) covers actual conduct of experiments and excludes post-production refinement, adaptation, reproduction, market research, routine QC testing, and end-user documentation.
26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(1), 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4), 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c), and IRS ATG Coordinated Issue Paper on technical writers / end-user manuals.
Direct Supervision (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2)) covers immediate technical supervision of qualified research and excludes administrative HR/financial management.

26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2) explicitly limits direct supervision to first-line management and excludes higher-level managers to whom first-line managers report (unless personally conducting or directly supervising research per Suder and IRS ATG).

Direct Support (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3)) covers services directly supporting persons conducting qualified research (machinist machining experimental model parts, secretary typing lab result reports, lab worker cleaning research equipment, clerk compiling research data) and excludes G&A even if housed in the R&D department.
26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3); IRS ATG Section 10 (Law in force, 2026)

All four positive examples and the G&A exclusions (payroll, accounting, general janitor, officer financial/HR supervision, in-house patent attorneys) appear in 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3) and IRS ATG. Under § 1.41-2(c)(3)(ii), Direct Support also includes services directly supporting persons who are directly supervising persons conducting qualified research.
Revamped Form 6765 requires upfront disclosure linking qualified employee wages to specific business components, and claims can face procedural disallowance for insufficient disclosure.
Form 6765 (Rev. Dec. 2024); Instructions (Rev. Dec. 2025); IRS Refund Claim FAQs (Updated June 18, 2024 & Oct. 1, 2026)

Form 6765 Section G Columns 50 (Direct Research), 51 (Direct Supervision), 52 (Direct Support), and 53 (Total Qualified Wages). Section G is optional for tax years beginning before 2026 and mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025; for amended refund claims (transition period through Jan. 10, 2027), FAQ 21 (June 18, 2024) waived listing individual employee names and discovery narratives at initial filing.

In Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, an engineering firm lost its claimed research credits because its activities were routine engineering / code compliance and failed to demonstrate a systematic Process of Experimentation (POE).
Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, Dkt. No. 4759-22 (Decided Dec. 23, 2024; Prior Order Aug. 29, 2023)

Holdings on IRC § 174 uncertainty, IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) POE, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2) shrink-back (cannot shrink back to design phases or individual employees), and 20% IRC § 6662 penalties. Procedural scope: the court ruled on a non-binding judgment sample of 3 trial projects (out of 238 claimed projects for credits generated in 2013–2016 and used in 2015–2019), rather than adjudicating all 238 projects on the merits.
Contemporaneous records carry greater weight than retrospective reconstruction.
26 U.S.C. § 6001; 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d) (T.D. 9104); 26 C.F.R. § 1.6001-1; IRS ATG Substantiation Chapter (Updated July 2, 2026); Little Sandy Coal, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023)

Per IRS ATG, the IRS is not required to accept estimates if documentation exists to verify actual expenses, and courts allow estimation (Cohan rule) only when contemporaneous records do not exist, the taxpayer first proves qualified research occurred under IRC § 41(d), and the lack of records is not a self-made inexactitude.
Wages taken into account in determining the Work Opportunity Credit under IRC § 51(a) are excluded from QRE wages (IRC § 41(b)(2)(D)(iii)).
26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(iii) & 26 U.S.C. § 51(a), § 51(b)(1)–(3); Form 6765 Section F, Line 42 (Law in force, 2026)
